title: Indra asks what the self is
hookLine: a god goes back to his teacher four times, and the last answer is about deep sleep
carry: even in deep sleep, the self is there
tomorrow: Arjuna says the mind is like the wind. what does Krishna say?

lines: A GOD AND A DEMON ASK THE SAME QUESTION.
VIROCHANA: THE SELF IS THE BODY.
cards: A god and a demon walk up to the same teacher. Indra, king of the gods, and Virochana, a prince of the asuras, both want one thing: to know the self. The teacher, Prajapati, has them live with him thirty-two years.
Then he says: dress in your finest, and look into a pan of water. What you see, that's the self. Virochana sees his own body, all dressed up, and goes home delighted: the self is the body.
Indra gets halfway home and stops. If the self is the body, it dies with the body. So he goes back.

teach.b: Thirty-two more years, and Prajapati says: the one who moves about in dreams, that's the self. Indra stops again. In dreams you can still be chased, still weep.
Back he goes. Thirty-two more: the one in deep, dreamless sleep, that's the self. And Indra: but then you know nothing at all, not even I am.
Five more years, and at last Prajapati tells him: the body is mortal, but it's the home of the self, which isn't; the self is the one who knows.
A hundred and one years of asking. Patanjali takes deep sleep seriously too.

Thread six sorts every turning of the mind into five kinds: right knowing; error, like the rope at dusk you take for a snake; imagination, words with nothing real behind them; sleep; and memory. Why is sleep on the list?
The commentary's answer: you wake up and say, I slept well. Something was there to know it.
Put the two together, the way many Vedanta teachers do, and you have a big Hindu teaching about the atman, the self: it isn't the body, or the dream, or the blank of deep sleep.

teach.h: THE SELF IS THERE THROUGH ALL THREE.
teach.b: It's the one who is there through all three. Teachers also use the five drawers in meditation. A worry at two in the morning is often imagination, not knowing.
Name the drawer, and it loosens.

how: Students of the Yoga Sutras often learn the five vrittis as a list and use them in meditation, noting which kind of thought is arising rather than following it; Hindu teachers often pair the list with the Upanishads' teaching that the self is the witness of waking, dream and deep sleep.

o: a guided rest done lying on the floor
a dream that shows you the future
sleep, counted as a turning of the mind

games.q: the god, the demon and the drawers — tap the pairs.
p: decided the self is the body
kept going back to ask again

s: Indra accepted Prajapati's first answer and went home happy
that was Virochana. Indra saw the problem and went back, again and again.
for Patanjali, deep sleep is a turning of the mind
you wake up remembering 'I slept well', so something was there to know it.
memory is one of Patanjali's five turnings
fifth on the list: holding on to what you've already experienced.

games.q: it's 2 a.m. and you're replaying a conversation that hasn't happened yet. which of Patanjali's drawers is it in?
o: imagination: a picture with nothing real behind it yet.
games.why: vikalpa, imagination: nothing real behind it yet. naming the drawer loosens it, and the one naming it is the self Indra was looking for.

practice: Let the mind do what it does, and when a thought comes, give it a drawer, softly: memory, imagination, knowing, error, or even sleep if you drift toward drowsiness.

You don't need to be right about the drawer; label it, let it go, and notice the one who is noticing, the way Indra kept asking who that was. If you pray, you can rest in that quiet with God; if not, simply rest.

wordCard.voice: Nidra, sleep, one of the five turnings of the mind. You wake and say, I slept well, and Hindu teachers say: then something was there.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sleep. Yoga Sutra 1.10 calls sleep the turning that rests on absence; 1.6 lists all five: pramana, viparyaya, vikalpa, nidra, smriti.

carryVoice: Your line: even in deep sleep, the self is there. Indra asked for a hundred and one years to learn it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 1.5–1.11 (the five turnings, painful and not painful)
Yoga Sutra 1.10 (abhava-pratyaya-alambana vrittir nidra: sleep rests on the experience of absence)
Vyasa's commentary on Yoga Sutra 1.10 (the waking memory 'I slept well' shows sleep is a turning)
Chandogya Upanishad 8.7–8.12 (Indra and Virochana with Prajapati: the self in the water, the dreamer, the deep sleeper; 32 + 32 + 32 + 5 = 101 years)
